analysis.one_liner: Bars new mining claims on more than a million acres of federal land around the Grand Canyon.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Natural Resources Committee; it was referred on March 3, 2011 and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently withdraw roughly 1,068,908 acres of federal land — the Tusayan Ranger District and Bureau of Land Management land near Kanab Creek and House Rock Valley in Arizona — from staking and patenting of mining claims and from mineral and geothermal leasing [S2][S3]. Under the nation's mining laws, anyone can stake a claim on open federal land and mine it; this bill would close that door on land that drains into the Grand Canyon, so no new mines could be opened there [S3]. People or companies who already held valid mining rights would keep them [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: People whose water depends on the Colorado River and its tributaries flowing through the Grand Canyon region, since a mining withdrawal keeps new mining waste and disruption out of the watersheds feeding the Canyon. Nearby communities whose economies rest on the Grand Canyon itself — tourism, outfitting, and the tribes in the region — also gain, because new industrial mining next to the park directly threatens what they sell and live near.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Water users and communities around the Grand Canyon

how_it_helps.text: Withdraws about 1,068,908 acres of federal land from location, entry, and patent under the mining laws, so no new mining claims could be staked there [S2][S3].
Also closes the land to mineral leasing, geothermal leasing, and mineral materials development, covering the other main ways extractive companies can gain rights to federal minerals [S2][S3].
Protects the land that drains into the Grand Canyon at its most sensitive point — the watersheds the title names — while respecting rights already validly held before the withdrawal [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mining companies and individuals who might otherwise stake claims or lease federal minerals on this land, and the communities that would have hosted the mining jobs and activity. The federal government also forgoes any minerals it could have sold or leased. The cost is concentrated and forgone, not a charge on anyone today.
analysis.who_pays_short: Uranium and hardrock mining claim holders

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal permanently forecloses domestic mineral production — including uranium, which mining supporters in the region argue is needed for energy and provides well-paid rural jobs in northern Arizona — on land that otherwise remains open to claim staking under the 1872 Mining Law. An honest supporter acknowledges this is a real tradeoff, not a free one.

Because the withdrawal is subject to valid existing rights, it does not stop mines on claims already staked before enactment; it only prevents future claims, so its protection is partial for existing operations [S3].

Support was thin: only the sponsor and two House Democrats cosponsored it, and no Republicans signed on, which made the bill's prospects in a mining-friendly committee effectively nil even before it sat unacted-upon [S4][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — keeping new mining out of the watersheds draining into the Grand Canyon — is large and permanent, and its cost falls on a concentrated group: mineral claim holders and the mining industry, plus some forgone rural jobs. The main honest objection is that a blanket withdrawal of over a million acres sweeps in more land than the most contamination-prone spots, and that a competing approach would allow regulated mining with modern safeguards on part of the area. On the substance, the protection it promised outweighs the forgone mineral value for most people who drink that water. As legislation, though, it accomplished nothing: the same core protection was later put in place administratively by the Obama administration in 2012, when the Interior Secretary ordered a 20-year withdrawal of about a million acres around the Grand Canyon — widely reported at the time — so the mining industry kept access only until executive action closed the door instead.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and split between two of its subcommittees on March 3, 2011, and then nothing ever happened to it — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until that Congress ended in January 2013 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva (D-AZ) introduced the bill on March 1, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1][S5].
Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands and the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
That was the last action of any kind; the bill received no markup, no hearing, and no floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining claim holders and uranium mining interests kept their access to the land, since no withdrawal ever passed. The loss to the public was partly offset two years later when the Interior Department imposed a similar 20-year withdrawal by executive action — a step that required no vote in Congress, and one that the next Congress or administration could reverse.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining interests; protection came later by executive order

for.name: Rep. Raúl M. Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Grand Canyon Watersheds Protection Act and shepherded it to referral in the Natural Resources Committee.

against.name: Rep. Doc Hastings
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or sent it to the floor, so it died there.

against.name: Uranium mining industry with claims near the Grand Canyon
against.role: Mining claim holders and exploration companies in northern Arizona
against.what_they_did: Opposed Grand Canyon-area mineral withdrawals, publicly and through litigation, as a threat to existing uranium projects in the region.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on, in a House where Republicans held the majority and controlled the committee calendar [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would bar staking new mining claims and leasing minerals across roughly 1.07 million acres around the Grand Canyon, eliminating future mines in the region (existing valid claims continue) [S2][S3]. Mining in these watersheds poses contamination risks to the Colorado River, which tens of millions of people drink from, so the industry's access to the land runs directly against water users' interests.

By keeping new mining development out of the drainages around the park, the withdrawal protects the scenery and water quality the regional tourism economy depends on. Visitors and local tourism businesses gain together.
